title: Artificial intelligence and wearable sensors in sports injury risk prediction: current status and future perspectives

sections.title: Introduction

paragraphs.en: In the context of increasingly sophisticated elite sports and individualized physical training, effective sports injury risk management has emerged as a critical determinant of athlete longevity, team success, and the long-term sustainability of the sports industry [1]. Epidemiological studies have shown that musculoskeletal injuries are highly prevalent among professional athletes, with a substantial proportion experiencing acute or chronic injuries during a single season, although incidence rates may vary across different sports and competitive contexts. Common and clinically significant injuries include anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears [2], stress fractures, tendinopathies, and muscle strains, particularly in high-impact sports such as football, basketball, and gymnastics [3]. These injuries often cause significant interruptions in training and competition, and in severe cases, may lead to psychological distress, career stagnation, or even premature retirement [4,5]. Consequently, early identification of high-risk individuals and the implementation of predictive and targeted prevention strategies have become central challenges in contemporary sports medicine and performance science.

Traditionally, the prediction and assessment of injury risk in athletes have relied heavily on subjective observations by coaches, clinical judgment by rehabilitation experts, standardized functional tests (e.g. Functional Movement Screen, FMS), and self-reported questionnaires. While these methods offer practical value, they suffer from limited objectivity, poor reproducibility, and low adaptability to different sports and individual conditions [6,7]. Moreover, traditional assessments are typically based on static, discrete-time evaluations, which fail to capture the dynamic fluctuations of physiological load and recovery status throughout the training process [8]. Relying on isolated indicators such as heart rate, lactate concentration, or electromyography (EMG) data also provides only partial insights and overlooks the complex, nonlinear interactions among physical, physiological, and psychological factors [6]. The lagging and fragmented nature of these conventional approaches significantly constrains their effectiveness in building a ‘prediction-feedback-intervention’ loop that meets the demands of modern sports science.

From the perspective of injury causation theory, sports injuries are not triggered by a single risk factor but arise from the cumulative and interactive effects of intrinsic susceptibility and external load exposure over time [9]. Both the dynamic model of sport injury aetiology and the biopsychosocial model emphasize the multifactorial, recursive, and time-dependent nature of injury risk, highlighting that susceptibility evolves across repeated exposure cycles [10]. Within this theoretical framework, assessment approaches based on static or proxy risk indicators are limited in their ability to capture key processes such as physiological drift, micro-trauma accumulation, or changes in movement stability [11]. In contrast, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with wearable sensing technologies enables continuous, time-resolved monitoring of multiple factors that directly influence injury susceptibility, allowing individualized injury risk to be dynamically modeled and updated as stress–strain relationships evolve [12].

In recent years, the rapid development of wearable sensor technologies and AI algorithms has given rise to a new data-driven paradigm for injury risk prediction [13]. Utilizing inertial measurement units (IMUs), surface EMG, heart rate variability (HRV), and emerging flexible bioelectronic sensors, it is now possible to collect high-frequency, continuous, and non-invasive data on athletes’ kinematic, physiological, biochemical, and psychological status during training and competition [14]. At the same time, AI techniques – particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), graph neural networks (GNNs, capable of modeling structured relationships such as joint connectivity), and Transformer-based models – have demonstrated strong capabilities in processing complex, nonlinear, and time-dependent data [15,16]. Through the intelligent mining of multi-modal signals, these algorithms can uncover hidden risk patterns and dynamic trajectories associated with injury onset, enabling precise and personalized risk profiling. The integration of wearable sensing and AI modeling thus represents a major shift from traditional experience-based methods to objective, real-time, and scalable predictive systems, which are increasingly being implemented in professional sports teams, research institutions, and commercial athlete monitoring platforms [17].

Despite its promise, this emerging field still faces significant challenges. First, most current studies focus on isolated sensors or single-model applications, lacking a comprehensive evaluation framework that integrates heterogeneous data sources [15]. Second, existing models often suffer from limited generalizability and interpretability when applied across different sports, training loads, or individual profiles [18]. Third, data standardization remains inadequate, and issues such as poor device compliance, inconsistent data quality, and privacy concerns further hinder large-scale deployment [19]. Additionally, ethical risks related to biometric data usage and athlete consent have not been fully addressed, raising concerns about the responsible implementation of these technologies [20].

Against this backdrop, this review aims to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of recent advances in wearable sensor technologies and AI-driven models for sports injury risk prediction. It seeks to offer a structured, forward-looking reference for researchers and practitioners in sports medicine, intelligent sensing, AI-based modeling, and rehabilitation engineering, while accelerating the translation of predictive technologies into real-world applications across elite sports, clinical rehabilitation, and broader health management domains.

sections.title: Methods

paragraphs.en: This review was conducted as a narrative review to systematically synthesize studies examining the application of AI and wearable sensors in sports injury risk prediction. Literature searches were performed in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus, covering publications up to August 2025. Search terms included, but were not limited to, ‘wearable sensors’, ‘sports injury prediction’, ‘artificial intelligence’, ‘machine learning’, ‘deep learning’, ‘IMU’, and ‘electromyography’, alone or in combination. Only articles published in English were considered. Studies focusing solely on single physiological measurements, lacking clearly defined injury-related outcomes, or with limited relevance to sports injury prediction were excluded. The final selection of articles was based on their relevance to the review topic, methodological clarity, and overall academic representativeness.

To enhance methodological transparency, the academic representativeness of included studies was evaluated based on the following criteria: (1) sample size and population diversity, (2) clarity of injury outcome definition, (3) use of multimodal data sources, and (4) methodological rigor of AI modeling. The literature screening process is shown in Figure 1.

sections.title: Current status and applications of wearable sensor technology
Types and development trends of wearable sensors

paragraphs.en: In recent years, wearable sensor technology has made rapid progress in the field of sports injury risk assessment. It has evolved from monitoring single physiological parameters to supporting multi-modal, integrated tracking of physiological, biomechanical, and psychological states. Based on their sensing targets and underlying principles, wearable sensors can be broadly categorized into the following types:

First, IMUs are currently the most widely used kinematic sensors. They typically consist of tri-axial accelerometers, gyroscopes, and magnetometers, enabling high-frequency tracking of displacement, velocity, angular acceleration, and other biomechanical parameters across various body segments [21]. IMUs are commonly used to capture gait characteristics, jump-landing mechanics, joint angle changes, and impact forces – all of which are closely associated with injury risk [22]. These devices are usually worn on the waist, ankles, or knees in fixed modules, offering good stability and continuous data acquisition during real-world movement [23].

Second, surface EMG sensors measure electrical signals generated during muscle contractions in real time, reflecting muscle activation patterns, fatigue trends, and bilateral coordination. These features are critical for identifying risks such as muscular imbalances and overuse injuries [24]. In recent years, studies have increasingly combined EMG data with motion recognition algorithms. For example, EMG signals can be transformed into time–frequency representations (e.g. via short-time Fourier transform or wavelet transform) to construct spectrogram-based features, which are then processed using deep learning models such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for pattern recognition[25]. This approach has shown promise in improving the early detection of muscle fatigue and micro-injury [26].

The third category includes physiological and mechanical sensors, which continuously monitor variables such as HR, HRV, skin temperature, sweat conductivity, and blood oxygen saturation. These indicators help assess internal load, autonomic nervous system activity, and recovery status [14,27]. In addition, pressure and force sensors (e.g. piezoelectric, strain gauge, and capacitive sensors) are widely used to monitor plantar pressure distribution, ground reaction forces, and gait asymmetry – parameters that are strongly associated with lower-limb impact stress and fatigue-related bone injuries [28]. These sensors are typically embedded in chest straps, wristbands, insoles, or smart footwear, offering both portability and real-time feedback [29].

The fourth category comprises flexible electronic sensors and smart textile-based sensors, which have gained momentum in recent years. These systems are built on conductive polymers and nanocomposite materials that adhere closely to the skin or clothing, enabling high-sensitivity detection of subtle physiological signals such as muscle tremors and microvascular fluctuations. Their stretchability, flexibility, and biocompatibility significantly enhance comfort and signal fidelity under dynamic training conditions [30]. However, during high-velocity movements, signal quality may be compromised due to motion artifacts and unstable skin–sensor interfaces, leading to reduced signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), which remains a key limitation for their reliable use in real-world field settings [31]. Emerging commercial products such as smart insoles, knee braces, and compression garments have successfully integrated flexible mechanical and physiological sensors to monitor joint impact loads, dynamic stability, and muscle fatigue levels, demonstrating strong potential for real-world applications [32].

Additionally, with the increasing degree of technological integration, multi-sensor fusion systems are becoming a dominant trend. For instance, modular wearable systems that combine IMU, EMG, and heart rate sensors can collect synchronized, multi-channel data, enhancing multi-dimensional perception of athletic performance and load. Some advanced systems are also equipped with Bluetooth and cloud-based interfaces, supporting remote data synchronization and real-time AI-based analytics, thereby laying the foundation for intelligent modeling frameworks [14,33].

Overall, wearable sensor development is moving toward lightweight, flexible, multi-modal, and wireless designs. Future advancements are expected in material innovation, energy efficiency, biocompatibility, and data transmission reliability. In addition, the establishment of standardized assessment protocols for both sensor performance and AI algorithms is essential to ensure reliability and comparability in real-world field applications [34]. As sensor systems continue to integrate with AI algorithms, the creation of adaptive and high-sensitivity platforms for intelligent injury risk monitoring will become a key direction in the field of wearable technology for sports science.

sections.title: Key monitoring indicators relevant to sports injury risk

paragraphs.en: The value of wearable sensing lies not just in data collection, but in converting signals into biologically meaningful indicators of neuromuscular function, physiological stress, and recovery status. These indicators are commonly categorized as kinematic, physiological/metabolic, and psycho-physiological, each reflecting a distinct layer of an athlete’s movement, internal load, and adaptation. Together, they underpin modern frameworks for sports injury risk assessment.

Kinematic indicators are pivotal in wearable-based injury prediction, as they reflect real-world mechanical load and movement stability. Patterns such as excessive knee valgus during landing, high impact peaks, gait asymmetry, and prolonged eccentric braking have been linked to elevated risks of ACL injuries, stress fractures, and muscle strains. These abnormalities often signal impaired proprioception, delayed neuromuscular response, or uneven force distribution, compromising joint stability under dynamic load [35]. For instance, studies on football athletes show a strong correlation between knee valgus and ACL injury, while gait asymmetry and abnormal plantar pressure have been identified as early predictors of tibial stress fractures in runners [36]. Real-time biomechanical monitoring thus enables early detection of risky movement strategies and supports targeted intervention.

Internal physiological and metabolic markers often deteriorate before clinical injury signs appear. Metrics like HR and HRV indicate autonomic balance, where persistent HRV reduction reflects incomplete recovery and links to overtraining, inflammation, and muscle breakdown [37]. Skin temperature changes can signal local inflammation, while sweat biomarkers – such as lactate, electrolytes, and pH – offer non-invasive insights into metabolic and hydration status [38]. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) enables real-time monitoring of muscle oxygen saturation (SmO₂), detecting early microcirculatory dysfunction and hypoxia that precede fatigue and strain injuries. However, the reliability of NIRS measurements may be influenced by limited light penetration depth and tissue composition, which can affect signal accuracy across athletes with different body types [39]. In endurance athletes, combined tracking of HR, HRV, and SmO₂ helps identify early signs of cardiovascular and muscular overload [40].

Psycho-physiological factors are increasingly recognized as key contributors to injury risk. High training loads and competitive pressure can disrupt sleep, elevate stress, and destabilize mood – activating the HPA axis, raising cortisol, impairing immunity, and delaying tissue repair [41]. These effects are often overlooked in conventional monitoring. Wearables combining HRV, actigraphy, and skin conductance now enable continuous assessment of sleep quality, stress, and autonomic balance. In professional basketball, reduced sleep quality over a week has been linked to higher lower-limb injury rates, while psychological stress before competition correlates with increased injury incidence in rugby [42,43]. These findings support integrating mental state tracking into injury prevention systems.

With the advancement of wearable technologies, simultaneous integration of kinematic, physiological, and psycho-physiological indicators is becoming increasingly feasible. For instance, combining IMU and EMG improves assessment of joint stability and muscle activation; HR and NIRS provide insights into both cardiovascular strain and local oxygenation; and incorporating stress and sleep metrics addresses gaps in physiological-only datasets. This multidimensional approach enriches AI model inputs by expanding feature space and improving signal quality, supporting more personalized and accurate injury prediction, as detailed in the next chapter.

In summary, kinematic, physiological/metabolic, and psycho-physiological indicators constitute the key information layers in sensor-based injury risk monitoring. By capturing the interplay between mechanical loading, internal homeostasis, and mental resilience, these indicators support the development of predictive frameworks that enable early detection and targeted intervention before overt injuries occur.

sections.title: Applied contexts and field deployments of wearable injury monitoring systems

paragraphs.en: As wearable sensor technologies advance, their use in sports injury risk management is expanding from research to elite training and commercial settings. Varying sports, performance levels, and training environments impose distinct requirements on sensor design and system integration.

High-impact sports like football, basketball, and rugby involve frequent cutting, landings, and collisions – common causes of knee, ankle, and soft tissue injuries. Professional teams increasingly use commercial multi-sensor systems, such as Catapult GPS-IMU vests, to monitor acceleration, sprint load, and movement volume for fatigue management [44]. These systems support structured training plans and help reduce injury risks from cumulative fatigue and sudden load spikes. Some teams also integrate biosensors, including EMG patches and HRV monitors [45], for deeper insight into neuromuscular fatigue and autonomic regulation, improving recovery and load adjustment decisions.

In endurance sports like marathon running, cycling, and swimming, wearable systems are widely used for continuous physiological monitoring and gait anomaly detection. Prolonged repetitive movements in endurance sports often lead to fatigue-related asymmetries and subtle biomechanical breakdowns. Recent studies have shown that smart insoles equipped with IMUs and pressure sensors can detect early gait asymmetry – often within the first few kilometers – which predicts subsequent fatigue-related instability and technique deviation [46]. Combined with pacing and environmental data, these systems support personalized training and injury prevention.

In major competitions, dense match schedules and psychological stress elevate acute injury risk. During the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, several national teams deployed integrated multi-sensor systems for real-time monitoring, including GPS tracking, EMG-based fatigue analysis, sleep tracking, and stress assessment [47]. These platforms supported both pre-competition risk evaluation and post-match recovery planning, demonstrating the multi-dimensional role of wearables in elite performance management.

Beyond professional settings, commercial wearables are increasingly used in elite and recreational sports. Devices like the WHOOP band, Oura Ring, and Polar chest strap now provide HR, HRV, sleep quality scores, strain indices, and recovery recommendations via intuitive interfaces [48]. Some systems integrate with load management platforms (e.g. CoachMe, TrainingPeaks), enabling data-driven training adjustments and real-time feedback [37]. Among youth and amateur athletes, these tools support individualized programming and proactive injury prevention.

Overall, wearable sensors have shown value across diverse sports, levels, and training contexts. They enhance injury risk detection, optimize load management, and support tailored recovery (Table 1). However, practical challenges remain – including device adherence, comfort, data integrity, and feedback latency – which must be addressed in future deployments.

sections.title: Advances in AI methods for sports injury risk prediction
Traditional machine learning methods in sports injury risk prediction

paragraphs.en: Traditional ML remains a widely used approach in sports injury risk prediction, particularly where data are structured, sample sizes are limited, and computational resources are constrained. These models are valued for their efficiency, interpretability, and practicality in early-stage or small-scale research.

Traditional ML models typically rely on handcrafted features extracted from time-series sensor data. Algorithms such as logistic regression (LR), support vector machines (SVM), random forests (RF), and gradient boosting methods are commonly employed to classify risk levels or predict injury outcomes. These models perform well when input data are structured, noise is manageable, and domain-specific knowledge is available to guide feature engineering [49].

In practice, sensor-derived features from IMUs, EMG, and HRV are often used. For example, RF and SVM models have successfully classified ACL injury risk using metrics like peak vertical ground reaction force and gait symmetry indices [50]. In endurance sports, logistic regression has been applied to HRV trends, stride frequency changes, and skin temperature variability to predict fatigue-related injuries [51]. Gradient boosting models, due to their ability to capture nonlinearities and feature interactions, have shown high predictive power in multi-modal fusion tasks. For example, XGBoost has been successfully used to classify neuromuscular recovery states using IMU and EMG data [52].

However, traditional ML has limitations. Performance depends heavily on the quality of feature engineering, and these methods struggle with unstructured, high-dimensional, or sequential data such as raw EMG or high-frequency IMU signals. Their generalizability across heterogeneous, real-world environments is also limited.

In sum, traditional ML remains a valuable tool in wearable-based injury risk modeling, particularly in low-resource or controlled settings. Yet, as data become more complex, DL methods offer increasing advantages.

sections.title: Deep learning methods and temporal modeling in injury risk prediction

paragraphs.en: As wearable sensor data become increasingly high-dimensional, heterogeneous, and temporally dynamic, traditional ML models are limited in their capacity to represent sequence-level information and capture complex patterns. In contrast, DL has emerged as a powerful alternative for sports injury risk prediction, offering automatic feature extraction from raw data and superior performance on structured, sequential, and multi-modal inputs. These characteristics make DL architectures particularly suitable for modeling the dynamic training–recovery–adaptation processes observed in real-world sports settings, where injury risk arises from the cumulative interaction of multiple factors over time rather than from isolated events. Importantly, these approaches enable the translation of wearable-derived signals into representations of underlying biomechanical processes, such as dynamic joint stability, neuromuscular coordination, and fatigue accumulation, thereby providing a mechanistic basis for injury risk prediction and supporting more interpretable modeling frameworks.

CNNs have demonstrated strong performance in processing spatially structured inputs such as pose heatmaps, joint angle maps, and visual kinematic data [53]. For example, CNNs have been applied to video-based assessments of gait and landing mechanics to detect ACL injury–prone movement patterns by analyzing spatial features derived from joint trajectories and body posture frames [54].

For temporally structured wearable data – such as HRV trends, EMG bursts, and IMU-derived accelerometry – Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and their variants, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) models, have been widely used to capture time-dependent risk factors [25,55]. These models are particularly well-suited to modeling fatigue–recovery–retraining cycles, enabling longitudinal tracking of overuse injury risks and early identification of chronic soft tissue stress.

More recently, Transformer architectures, initially developed for natural language processing, have shown promise in modeling long-range dependencies in physiological time series. Their attention-based mechanisms allow for flexible handling of high-frequency sensor streams and multi-week training histories without relying on sequential computation [55]. Pilot studies have explored the integration of IMU data, HRV metrics, and subjective wellness scores into Transformer-based models to generate personalized, temporally aware injury risk forecasts [16].

In cases where wearable data exhibit underlying spatial or anatomical structures – such as biomechanical joint connectivity or skeletal kinematics – GNNs have been introduced to model node-level (e.g. joint angles) and edge-level (e.g. coordination patterns) relationships. For instance, dynamic graphs constructed from IMU-derived pelvic, knee, and ankle joint angles can be used by GNNs to identify inter-joint coordination anomalies that may precede loss of stability and elevated injury susceptibility [56]. However, compared with traditional fixed skeletal models, dynamic graph representations often involve higher computational complexity and increased processing demands, which may limit their efficiency in real-time or resource-constrained applications [57]. In this context, graph nodes typically correspond to specific anatomical joints (e.g. hip, knee, and ankle), while edges represent biomechanical or functional relationships between joints, such as kinematic coupling or coordination patterns during movement. This formulation enables complex inter-joint interactions to be explicitly modeled in a manner that is intuitive and interpretable for biomechanical and clinical applications [58].

A major challenge in deep injury modeling is the scarcity of labeled data, due to the relatively low incidence of injury events and the difficulty of collecting long-term, high-resolution sensor datasets. To mitigate this, Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have been adopted to pretrain DL models on unlabeled data using pretext tasks such as temporal order prediction or masked signal reconstruction [59]. These methods enable models to learn transferable representations, which can be fine-tuned on limited labeled datasets, improving generalization across different sports and athlete populations [60]. For example, recent studies have applied SSL to IMU-based gait analysis, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting gait events from smartphone sensor data without extensive manual annotation, thereby addressing key challenges in real-world sports monitoring [61].

It should be noted that sports injury prediction tasks are typically characterized by a pronounced class imbalance due to the low incidence of injury events, which can limit the stability and generalizability of deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks and Transformer-based architectures, in real-world applications [62,63]. To mitigate the bias introduced by the scarcity of injury samples, existing studies have explored various strategies, such as oversampling approaches (e.g. SMOTE), synthetic data generation, and the incorporation of cost-sensitive learning during model training to enhance sensitivity to injury events [64]. Overall, the application of synthetic data generation in sports injury prediction remains limited and controversial in clinically relevant contexts, with its effectiveness requiring further validation. Moreover, the performance of such approaches is highly dependent on data characteristics and validation strategies.

In summary, DL enables end-to-end modeling of complex and temporally rich wearable data, providing enhanced capacity for injury risk prediction compared to traditional ML. Despite these advances, ongoing challenges include limited interpretability, variability across real-world settings, and the need for cross-sport generalization – all of which must be addressed to facilitate large-scale deployment of DL systems in sports science and rehabilitation contexts.

sections.title: Representative research advances in AI-based injury risk prediction

paragraphs.en: In recent years, the combined advancement of wearable sensor precision and AI modeling capabilities has significantly accelerated the progress of sports injury risk prediction. Notably, substantial breakthroughs have been achieved in injuries with clearly defined risk mechanisms, including structural joint injuries, fatigue-related injuries, and chronic bone stress injuries.

sections.title: ACL injury prediction: dynamic instability and temporal modeling

paragraphs.en: ACL injuries typically occur during high-impact maneuvers such as rapid cutting or jump landings. These injuries are often preceded by subtle deficits in lower-limb coordination and neuromuscular control, which can manifest in aberrant kinematic signatures such as knee valgus dynamics during landing [65].

For example, Zaroug [66] applied Bi-LSTM models to IMU-derived angular velocity and acceleration data collected during jump-landing movements to predict biomechanical instability, showing superior temporal modeling compared to SVM and RF baselines. Similarly, Wang [67] summarized multiple AI-driven injury prediction frameworks, highlighting the advantage of Bi-LSTM models in capturing sequential dependencies within jump-landing tasks involving youth athletes. Such frameworks offer a promising pathway for identifying early biomechanical indicators – such as peak valgus acceleration shortly after ground contact – that may signal elevated injury risk, aligning with prior biomechanical insights. Collectively, these studies suggest that AI models do not merely classify injury risk, but fundamentally capture deficits in neuromuscular coordination and dynamic joint stability, which are core biomechanical mechanisms underlying ACL injury.

sections.title: Fatigue-related injury prediction: physiological drift and feature interaction

paragraphs.en: Unlike structural injuries, fatigue-induced conditions such as muscle strains and tendinopathies exhibit high inter-individual variability and dynamic progression. They are often driven by cumulative training load, inadequate recovery, and autonomic dysregulation [68], which require AI models to detect subtle physiological drifts and model nonlinear feature interactions.

A representative study involving Young Soccer Players collected multi-modal physiological data, including HRV fluctuations, EMG spectral features, and subjective workload ratings during training. These signals were used as inputs to train a ML classifier – such as XGBoost – to stratify short-term fatigue-related injury risk. The model demonstrated superior predictive capacity compared to single-feature threshold approaches, particularly in identifying minor muscle strains occurring within days of high-load sessions [69].

Notably, HRV decline rate and EMG median frequency shift emerged as dominant predictors of short-term fatigue-related injury risk, reflecting their ability to capture cumulative physiological stress and early fatigue signatures [70,71]. These findings further suggest that fatigue-related injuries are better understood as a manifestation of dynamic physiological dysregulation rather than isolated biomechanical abnormalities, underscoring the importance of integrating temporal, multimodal physiological signals into predictive models.

sections.title: Stress fracture prediction: chronic load mechanisms and cross-modal temporal fusion

paragraphs.en: Stress fractures represent a highly insidious class of overuse injuries, particularly prevalent among female endurance athletes. Their pathogenesis involves microtrauma accumulation from repetitive low-intensity loads, along with imbalances in bone remodeling, metabolic status, and recovery cycles [72]. Due to the absence of overt symptoms, effective prediction demands longitudinal, multi-modal data fusion across different timescales.

In recent modeling efforts, Wen et al. [16] proposed a multimodal Transformer framework for injury prediction that integrates biomechanical constraints with temporal attention mechanisms. Their system processed heterogeneous sensor data – such as IMU-derived gait metrics, HRV fluctuations, sleep quality scores, and self-reported fatigue levels – to identify emerging patterns of physiological stress in athletes.

Compared with baseline models such as LSTM and XGBoost, Transformer architectures are better suited for characterizing training–recovery dynamics in long-term time-series data. Attention-based Transformer models can highlight critical risk windows in longitudinal records that correspond to abrupt increases in training load or insufficient recovery, which are widely regarded as key precursors to bone stress injury. By assigning differential weights to distinct temporal segments, attention mechanisms provide informative temporal cues that support the early identification of chronic bone stress injury risk [73].

sections.title: Integrated applications of AI and wearable sensors

paragraphs.en: The deep integration of AI and wearable sensor technology is reshaping the landscape of sports injury risk management. Traditionally, injury risk assessment relied on single-parameter monitoring, intermittent data sampling, and expert judgment. Today, AI-driven systems enable the fusion of large-scale, real-time, and multi-source data streams, transitioning injury prediction from isolated metrics to dynamic and system-level modeling. This evolution represents a critical step toward closed-loop injury prevention, in which continuous status monitoring, risk identification, and timely intervention are tightly integrated. Within this framework, systems increasingly incorporate real-time behavioral signals – such as movement adaptations and fatigue-induced gait changes – into AI-driven prediction and feedback loops, enabling dynamic adjustment of injury risk assessment and intervention strategies. In such systems, model outputs are not only used for risk forecasting but can also be linked to immediate feedback mechanisms – for example, providing haptic or visual feedback to prompt real-time correction of landing mechanics when high-risk movement patterns are detected – thereby enabling responsive, adaptive injury prevention strategies (Figure 2).

At the heart of this transformation lies the ability to fuse multimodal data into a coherent framework. Sports injuries rarely stem from a single factor; instead, they often result from the synergistic failure of physiological, biomechanical, and even psychological systems. Single-sensor approaches frequently fall short in capturing these latent interactions. Multimodal fusion, in contrast, allows for a comprehensive risk portrait by detecting cross-domain signal interplay. For example, Wang et al. [74] developed a wearable-enabled system combining inertial and heart rate sensors with Transformer modeling, reporting injury risk prediction accuracy close to 90% in training load optimization tasks. This study highlights the emerging potential of attention-based architectures in identifying subtle risk shifts before symptomatic onset.

Building upon such foundations, real-time prediction and intelligent feedback are becoming the new norm in high-performance environments. AI-powered systems are now capable of streaming sensor data, conducting real-time inference, and delivering individualized risk scores within minutes. Hu et al. [75] developed an IoT-enabled platform that streams EMG, heart rate, and gait data to an edge computing unit for real-time fatigue assessment and automatic feedback to coaching staff. The system recommends training load adjustments when moderate-to-high risk levels are detected, supporting proactive recovery strategies. In more cutting-edge cases, such predictions are linked to active feedback mechanisms – such as vibrating wearables or augmented-reality glasses – that guide athletes to self-correct movement patterns in real-time. A notable example from alpine skiing involved real-time detection of suboptimal landing mechanics, which triggered haptic feedback to encourage immediate technical correction, thus shifting injury prevention from passive observation to active intervention [76].

As these technologies mature, real-world deployments are moving from pilot studies to standard practice. The Australian national team has been among the early adopters of AI-integrated athlete monitoring systems. In elite training contexts, researchers have applied wearable technologies and data analytics to predict sports injuries and optimize training loads in real time [19,77]. In China, initiatives such as the ‘Digital Twin Athlete’ program are being trialed, combining 3D biomechanical modeling, longitudinal physiological response data, and predictive AI to simulate and optimize individual training scenarios [53]. These systems provide a virtual testbed for scenario planning, risk assessment, and load management, offering data-driven support for complex training decisions. However, despite these advances, most current implementations are better understood as advanced data-driven monitoring and simulation platforms rather than fully realized digital twin systems, as key features such as real-time bidirectional integration and continuous system updating remain under development.

Together, these examples underscore that AI–wearable integration is no longer a conceptual innovation but a functional, deployable system with tangible benefits. The core shift lies in transitioning injury prediction from static post-event assessments to dynamic, forward-looking control systems – systems capable of early detection, personalized feedback, and adaptive intervention. With continued advancements in flexible sensors, on-device computing, and self-learning algorithms, the future of sports injury prevention lies in intelligent, real-time, and context-aware solutions – not merely in collecting data, but in making sense of it, and acting on it, in the moments that matter most.

sections.title: Current limitations and future directions
Technical challenges in data integration and modeling

paragraphs.en: Although the integration of AI and wearable sensor technologies has demonstrated significant potential in sports injury risk prediction, the translation from laboratory validation to real-world implementation remains fraught with multidimensional challenges. A major technical barrier is data heterogeneity and the lack of standardization. Wearable devices from different manufacturers vary considerably in sampling frequency, sensor accuracy, data formats, and communication protocols. These discrepancies can lead to substantial shifts in feature distributions, resulting in significant performance degradation when models are transferred across devices or settings. Recent multicenter evidence showed that integrating gait and HRV data from five different devices caused more than a 25% reduction in model performance due to inconsistent signal characteristics [78]. To address this issue, the development of standardized data processing frameworks – such as sensor fusion algorithms, cross-device calibration strategies, and unified data formatting protocols – has been proposed to improve interoperability and model robustness across heterogeneous devices [14,78]. However, this challenge has accelerated the development of interoperable data formats, open APIs, and unified timestamp protocols, laying the groundwork for scalable, cross-device injury prediction systems. Equally significant is the issue of model interpretability, which limits the adoption of AI models in practical coaching and clinical settings. Coaches and medical professionals often care less about who is at risk, and more about why. Yet most high-performing models – such as LSTMs or Transformers – function as ‘black boxes’ and offer limited transparency. In response, explainable AI (XAI), which aims to improve the transparency of model predictions by identifying factors contributing to decision-making, is increasingly being adopted. For example, attention-weighted visualization methods can highlight influential time segments or physiological markers [16]. Despite these advances, an important challenge remains the clinical validation of model explanations. In many current studies, attention weights or feature attribution maps are used to infer which temporal segments or physiological variables contribute most to injury risk predictions [79]. However, such explanations do not inherently guarantee alignment with established biomechanical or clinical risk factors. For instance, attention highlighted by Transformer-based models may emphasize specific time windows without necessarily corresponding to known injury-related mechanisms, such as excessive knee valgus loading or maladaptive neuromuscular control [79,80]. Emerging approaches such as physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which incorporate biomechanical constraints and prior physiological knowledge into model training, may help improve the biological plausibility and interpretability of predictions [81]. Therefore, greater emphasis should be placed on validating explainable AI outputs against established biomechanical indicators, expert annotations, and multimodal evidence to ensure their clinical relevance.

sections.title: User-related challenges and adoption in practice

paragraphs.en: Another longstanding barrier is limited model generalizability due to inter-individual variability. Athletes differ substantially in age, biomechanics, training load, hormonal cycles, and recovery patterns, which often causes population-level models to fail in personalized applications. Moreover, sports injury prediction studies are frequently constrained by small cohort sizes and low event rates, increasing the risk of overfitting, where models perform well during training or internal validation but fail to generalize to independent datasets or real-world settings. To address this, recent approaches have employed adaptive learning techniques – including self-supervised representation learning and few-shot personalization strategies – to enable models to recalibrate with minimal user-specific data [82]. User-related issues also affect system reliability. Low compliance rates and sensor discomfort can compromise data quality, even if the prediction models themselves are sound. In a real-world deployment, athletes with <70% sensor compliance had over 25% higher prediction error rates [31]. This has led to increased investment in flexible electronics, miniaturized modules, and non-invasive skin-conforming designs. More importantly, strategies from behavioral psychology are being integrated to improve athlete engagement and long-term adoption, shifting AI systems from externally imposed tools to actively accepted training partners.

sections.title: Privacy and data protection in wearable-AI systems

paragraphs.en: Finally, the protection of data privacy and ethical concerns further complicate deployment, particularly when dealing with sensitive physiological and psychological information. Data misuse – such as unauthorized monitoring of psychological fatigue – could lead to mistrust and ethical breaches. To mitigate this, techniques such as federated learning and differential privacy are being explored. These methods allow models to be trained locally without uploading raw data, and introduce noise to outputs to ensure user anonymity, achieving a delicate balance between data utility and privacy preservation.

sections.title: Future perspectives for wearable-AI injury prevention

paragraphs.en: Within these constraints lie the seeds of transformation. The future of wearable-AI systems in sports injury prevention lies not in making predictions more accurate alone, but in making them interpretable, responsive, secure, and individualized. Multimodal data fusion will continue to evolve, enabling panoramic views of physiological, biomechanical, and cognitive states. Digital twin athlete models will become central platforms in elite sports training, injury simulation, and rehabilitation planning. Real-time alerts and closed-loop interventions – via haptic feedback, edge computing, or AR guidance – will drive instantaneous behavioral responses [83]. XAI-enabled visual dashboards will bridge the gap between model outputs and human decision-making, improving acceptance among coaches and clinicians. Beyond musculoskeletal injuries, future research may extend AI–wearable frameworks to concussion-related applications, including the use of instrumented mouthguards or cervical motion sensors to capture both linear and rotational head dynamics, as well as to support monitoring of recovery processes.

sections.title: Conclusion

paragraphs.en: This review synthesizes recent advancements in wearable sensor technologies and AI algorithms for sports injury risk prediction, highlighting their growing role in transforming athlete monitoring from subjective, intermittent assessments to objective, continuous, and data-driven frameworks. By integrating kinematic, physiological, and psycho-physiological indicators, wearable sensors offer comprehensive insights into biomechanical loading, internal stress responses, and psychological resilience. Concurrently, machine learning and deep learning models – particularly those designed for temporal, multimodal, and biomechanically informed data – have demonstrated strong potential for identifying early warning patterns that precede injury.

Together, these developments mark a paradigm shift toward proactive, personalized, and real-time injury prevention. While significant challenges remain, ongoing progress in sensor innovation, interpretable AI, privacy-preserving computation, and digital twin technologies is paving the way for next-generation intelligent monitoring systems. Ultimately, the convergence of AI and wearable sensing has the potential to evolve into an integrated decision-support ecosystem that enhances athlete safety, optimizes training load, and supports long-term performance sustainability across both elite and recreational sports settings.
